exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```swift
var s = ""
for i in stride(from: 1, through: 9, by: 3) {
    s += String(i)
}
print(s)
```

feedback.message: Close. `through:` includes the end value when the stride lands on it... does it land on 9? Count 1, 4, 7, 10.

hints: List the values: start at 1 and add 3 while you stay at or below 9.
`String(i)` turns each number into text, and `+=` appends it.
exercises.solution: The stride produces 1, 4 and 7 (the next value, 10, is past 9). Each is appended to `s` as text, so the program prints `147`. With `stride(from:to:by:)` the result would be the same here, because 9 itself is never reached.

feedback.message: Not yet. Did you count 0? It is in the range and 0 % 3 is 0.

hints: Which of those leave remainder 0 when divided by 3?
exercises.solution: The half-open range gives 0 to 9, and the `where` clause keeps those divisible by 3: 0, 3, 6 and 9. The body runs **4** times.

feedback.message: Not yet. (0, 0) does satisfy `a == -b`, but cases are tried in order and the first match wins.

hints: Try each case in order, top to bottom, for each point.
(0, 0) matches more than one case. Which comes first?
exercises.solution: (0, 0) matches `(_, 0)` first: **x-axis**. (3, −3) is not on either axis, and 3 == −(−3), so it is **anti-diagonal**. (0, 4) fails the first case and matches `(0, _)`: **y-axis**. The line is `x-axis anti-diagonal y-axis`.

feedback.message: Close. Check i = 3, j = 3: 9 > 6, so `break outer` leaves both loops before counting.

hints: `continue outer` skips straight to the next `i`.
`break outer` ends both loops at once. Trace i = 1, 2, 3 carefully.
exercises.solution: For i = 1: j = 1 counts (1); j = 2 > i, so `continue outer`. For i = 2: j = 1 and j = 2 count (3); j = 3 continues outer. For i = 3: j = 1 counts (4), j = 2 gives 6, not more than 6, so it counts (5); j = 3 gives 9 > 6 and `break outer` ends everything. The program prints **5**.

exercises.prompt:
What does this program print?

```swift
var n = 100
repeat {
    n /= 3
} while n > 5
print(n)
```

feedback.message: Not yet. After n becomes 11 the condition `11 > 5` is still true, so the body runs once more.

hints: The condition is checked after each pass of the body.

options.label: It prints all 4 elements.
options.feedback: Not yet. `0...4` is a closed range: it includes 4.

options.label: It prints the 4 elements, then the program stops with an index-out-of-range trap.
options.feedback: Yes. The last index is 3, and arrays check every subscript.

options.label: It prints the 4 elements and then a garbage value.
options.feedback: Not yet. That is what C might do. Swift checks array bounds and traps instead of reading past the end.

options.label: It does not compile.
options.feedback: Not yet. The compiler cannot know how many elements `items` will have at run time, so it accepts the loop.

hints: What are the valid indices of a 4-element array?
exercises.solution: `0...items.count` is `0...4`, which includes 4, but the valid indices are 0 to 3. The first four iterations print the elements; the fifth subscripts with 4 and the program traps. Write `0..<items.count`, `items.indices`, or simply `for item in items`.

exercises.prompt: Your team's code has a `switch` over an enum you own, with a `default:` case that logs "unexpected". A colleague adds a new case to the enum. What is the main cost of that `default`?

options.label: The new case is silently handled by `default`, so the compiler cannot point out that this switch needs updating.
options.feedback: Yes. Without `default`, the switch would stop compiling, which is exactly the reminder you want.

options.label: `default` makes the switch slower.
options.feedback: Not yet. Performance is not the issue; the lost compile-time check is.

options.label: The program will not compile.
options.feedback: Not yet. With `default`, it still compiles. That is the problem.

options.label: There is no cost: `default` is always good practice.
options.feedback: Not yet. For integers and strings it is necessary, but for your own enums it hides missing cases.

hints: What does exhaustiveness checking do when a case is missing and there is no `default`?
exercises.solution: Exhaustiveness checking makes a switch that misses a case fail to compile. A `default` satisfies the check forever, so the new case flows into it unnoticed. Listing every case of your own enums lets the compiler give you a to-do list whenever the enum grows.
